```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(ggplot2)
  library(knitr)
})

kOutputDir <- file.path("..", "output", "omip39")

ReadOutput <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path(kOutputDir, name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    stop(
      "The analysis output is missing: ", path, "\n",
      "Run every script from 02 to 05 first. See the section 'Reproducing this'."
    )
  }
  read.csv(path, check.names = FALSE)
}

OutputImage <- function(name) {
  file.path(kOutputDir, name)
}
```

## Why this dataset

The PBMC report showed that an automated template gates a whole experiment from
one text file. It did not show whether the template lands where an expert lands,
because there was nothing to compare against.

OMIP-39 fixes that. It is a published panel for human adaptive NKG2C+ natural
killer cells [1], and its FlowRepository deposit ships the FlowJo workspace the
authors used. The manual result therefore does not come from this project. The
same donor file is gated twice, once by the authors in FlowJo and once here by an
openCyto template, and the two frequencies sit side by side.

The deposit also ships twelve single stained controls, so compensation can be
computed from scratch rather than taken from the file. That turned out to be the
part with the finding in it.

The report has five parts. Compensation computed from the controls, automated
gating from a template, that template compared against the published manual gates,
the paper's own claims tested against the deposited data, and clustering as a third
route to the same populations.

```{r}
#| label: dataset

match_table <- ReadOutput("control_match_table.csv")
kable(
  match_table[, c("stain", "channel", "marker", "matched_by")],
  caption = "The twelve compensation controls, each matched to the channel it stains."
)
```

## Part 1: compensation

### Matching controls to channels

Every control file carries one stain, and that stain names one detector in the
panel. FlowJo makes a person do this matching in its interface. Here it is derived
from the marker names that the FCS files already carry.

The matching runs four passes, and each one exists because a real file broke the
pass before it.

```{r}
#| label: match-passes

passes <- as.data.frame(table(match_table$matched_by))
colnames(passes) <- c("pass", "controls")
kable(passes, caption = "How many controls each matching pass resolved.")
```

Read the passes as a ladder of tolerance. `exact` compares the two strings
character for character. `normalised` ignores case and punctuation. `collapsed`
removes every separator, which is what resolves `CD2 PerCP-Cy55` on the control
against `CD2 PerCPCy55` in the panel. `antibody` matches on the antibody name
alone and ignores the fluorochrome, which is what resolves `Zombie auqa CD14 CD19`
against `Zombie aqua CD14 CD19`. That last pair is a typo in the panel, and the
matcher reports which pass it used, so a weaker match is visible rather than
silent.

### Whether each control can support an estimate

A spillover value is a ratio between the signal a fluorochrome puts into its own
detector and the signal it puts into another one. Both terms need a positive
population to measure.

A bead control is almost entirely positive. A cell control is not, because a
marker that sits on a minority of cells leaves most events negative.

```{r}
#| label: control-quality

quality <- ReadOutput("control_quality.csv")
kable(
  quality[, c("stain", "positive_percent", "primary_is_brightest", "verdict")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Percentage of positive events per control, against a threshold set at the 99.9th percentile of the unstained control.",
  col.names = c("Control", "Positive, percent", "Brightest on its own detector", "Verdict")
)
```

Two things come out of this table.

Every control reads brightest on the detector it was matched to, so the matching
above is correct. The channel assignment is not the problem anywhere in this
dataset.

Four controls are positive on under 20 percent of their events. NKp30 is positive
on 3.5 percent and NKG2C on 7.0 percent. Those are real biology, since NKG2C marks
a small adaptive NK subset and that subset is the point of the paper. They are
still poor compensation controls.

### The finding: mode against median

`flowStats::spillover_ng()` defaults to `method = "mode"`. On a bead control the
mode is the positive peak, because nearly every event is positive. On a cell
control for a rare marker the mode is the negative peak, and the ratio it produces
does not describe spillover at all.

This was not obvious from the code. It appeared as a spillover value of 164
percent, which is not physical for that pair, so the cause had to be found.

The measurement below runs the computation under every combination of the three
relevant arguments and scores each result against the matrix the instrument stored
for this experiment. The stored matrix is a fair reference. It was built from these
same controls, by the acquisition software, with an operator checking it.

```{r}
#| label: method-sweep

sweep <- ReadOutput("method_sweep.csv")
kable(
  sweep,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Every configuration, scored against the stored matrix. Differences are in percentage points.",
  col.names = c("method", "pregate", "normFilter", "channels",
                "max difference", "median difference", "values above 100 percent",
                "correlation", "status")
)
```

Read the first and third rows against each other. Both pregate and both filter, and
only the summary statistic differs. The mode gives a correlation of 0.619 with the
stored matrix and produces two impossible values. The median gives 0.975 and
produces none.

The two impossible values under the mode came from NKG2C and NKG2A, which the
quality table above flags as positive on 7.0 percent and 17.2 percent of events.
The failure and the diagnostic point at the same two controls.

Three configurations returned no usable estimate at all, and the table records that
rather than dropping the row.

So the analysis uses `method = "median"`, and
`ComputeSpilloverFromControls()` carries that as its default with this measurement
in its documentation. The rule to take away is narrower than "use median": use the
mode when the controls are beads, and check the positive fraction before you trust
either.

### The computed matrix

```{r}
#| label: spillover-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Spillover computed from the twelve single stained controls. The diagonal is dropped, because it is 1 everywhere and would set the colour scale."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("spillover_heatmap.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: spillover-top

top <- ReadOutput("spillover_computed_top10.csv")
top$percent <- round(100 * top$spill, 2)
kable(
  top[, c("from", "to", "percent")],
  caption = "The ten largest computed spillover values.",
  col.names = c("From detector", "Into detector", "Spillover, percent")
)
```

### Computed against stored

```{r}
#| label: matrix-comparison

matrix_comparison <- ReadOutput("spillover_computed_vs_stored.csv")
kable(
  head(matrix_comparison, 10),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The ten pairs where the computed matrix disagrees most with the stored one. All values are percentages.",
  col.names = c("From", "Into", "Computed", "Stored", "Difference, points")
)
```

The two matrices agree closely in the middle and disagree at the top. The largest
gap is BV510 into the violet 450/50 detector. Both agree that this is the largest
spillover in the panel, and they disagree on its size.

That residual is worth naming rather than smoothing over. It is not resolved here,
and a real experiment would settle it by looking at that one pair on a plot before
choosing a matrix.

## Part 2: automated gating

The template mirrors the hierarchy the authors published.

```{r}
#| label: template

template <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "omip39_gating_template.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(
  template[, c("alias", "pop", "parent", "dims", "gating_method", "gating_args")],
  caption = "The gating template. Each row is one population."
)
```

The four quadrant populations are built differently from the way the analyst built
them. FlowJo drew one quadrant gate, which sets both cut points at once. The
template fits two one dimensional gates, on CD56 and on CD3 separately, and then
combines them with a boolean. The populations are defined the same way and the
cut points are found independently, so a difference between the two results can
come from that alone.

```{r}
#| label: automated-tree
#| fig-cap: "The hierarchy the template produced."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("automated_tree.png"))
```

## Part 3: the comparison

The published workspace holds 163 populations. Most are boolean combinations of
six markers below the CD56dim branch. This comparison covers the seven named
parent populations, which is where a difference means something. The mapping
between the two naming schemes is a judgement, so it lives in a file.

```{r}
#| label: population-map

population_map <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "omip39_population_map.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(
  population_map,
  caption = "How a manual population name maps to a template alias, and why."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison

comparison <- ReadOutput("comparison.csv")
kable(
  comparison[, c("manual", "automated", "manual_percent", "automated_percent",
                 "difference", "verdict")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Manual against automated, percent of parent, on one donor file.",
  col.names = c("Manual", "Automated", "Manual, percent", "Automated, percent",
                "Difference, points", "Verdict")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Each population once. The dashed line is exact agreement."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("comparison_scatter.png"))
```

### Where they agree and where they do not

Four of the seven populations agree within five percentage points. That tolerance
is a judgement made before the numbers were read, and it is not a published
standard.

The disagreement is not spread evenly. It starts at the singlet gate, where the
analyst kept 96.5 percent of viable events and the template kept 86.7 percent.
`openCyto::singletGate` fits a regression of FSC-H on FSC-A and cuts at a fixed
distance from it, while the analyst drew a polygon by eye and drew it wider.

Everything below inherits that. The template throws away roughly a tenth more
events at the singlet step, and the populations it counts afterwards are counted
out of a smaller and slightly different parent.

The lymphocyte gate then differs by 5.7 points in the same direction. By the CD56
against CD3 split the two methods are close again on the small populations, at 2.5
points and 1.4 points, and further apart on the largest one at 6.0 points.

## Part 4: reproducing the paper

The comparison above asks whether two analyses of one file agree. It does not ask
whether the paper's conclusions hold. That is a different question and the
deposited data can answer it.

OMIP-039 makes seven directional claims about how CD56dim NKG2C+ NK cells differ
from CD56dim NKG2C- NK cells, and it states one composite phenotype as prototypic
for adaptive NK cells. Each claim is recorded in a file with the sentence it came
from, so a reader can check the claim against the paper before checking the number
against the data.

```{r}
#| label: claims-file

claims <- read.csv(
  file.path("..", "gating", "omip39_paper_claims.csv"),
  check.names = FALSE
)
kable(
  claims[, c("claim_id", "marker", "measure", "direction", "figure")],
  caption = "The claims, as recorded. The quote column holds the sentence each one came from and is omitted here for width."
)
```

Each claim is tested twice, by two routes that share no gating decision.

### Route 1: the authors' own gates

The deposited workspace holds 64 boolean populations under each NKG2C branch,
which is Figure 1C. A boolean set partitions its parent, so the frequency of one
marker is the sum of the counts where that marker is positive. Deriving the
frequencies that way uses only the gates the authors drew and adds nothing.

```{r}
#| label: claims-manual

claims_manual <- ReadOutput("claims_manual.csv")
kable(
  claims_manual[, c("marker", "direction", "test_percent", "reference_percent",
                    "difference_points", "verdict")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The paper's claims, tested against its own gates.",
  col.names = c("Marker", "Paper expects", "NKG2C+ percent", "NKG2C- percent",
                "Difference, points", "Verdict")
)
```

All six frequency claims hold, and the differences are large. NKG2A falls by 41.8
percentage points and ILT2 rises by 21.7.

### Figure 1C, the prototypic adaptive phenotype

```{r}
#| label: phenotype

phenotype <- ReadOutput("adaptive_phenotype_manual.csv")
kable(
  phenotype,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The population NKG2A- NKp30- Siglec-7- ILT2+ CD57+ CD2+, in each NKG2C branch.",
  col.names = c("Branch", "Population", "Events", "Parent events",
                "Percent of parent")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: phenotype-enrichment
#| echo: false

enrichment <- phenotype$percent_of_parent[1] / phenotype$percent_of_parent[2]
cat(sprintf(
  "The prototypic phenotype is %.1f times as frequent in NKG2C+ as in NKG2C-.\n",
  enrichment
))
```

That ratio is the central claim of the paper, computed from the data the authors
deposited alongside it.

### Route 2: the automated template

```{r}
#| label: claims-automated

claims_automated <- ReadOutput("claims_automated.csv")
kable(
  claims_automated[, c("marker", "direction", "test_percent", "reference_percent",
                       "difference_points", "verdict")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "The same claims, tested against gates the template fitted from scratch.",
  col.names = c("Marker", "Paper expects", "NKG2C+ percent", "NKG2C- percent",
                "Difference, points", "Verdict")
)
```

Five of the six reproduce, with the same directions and comparable magnitudes.

The sixth does not, and the reason is a broken gate rather than a failed claim.
The automated NKp30 gate calls 100 percent of events positive in both branches, so
`mindensity` put its cut below the whole distribution. The claim is reported as
"too small to call" rather than dropped, because a silent omission would read as
agreement. That gate needs a bounded search range and it has not been fixed.

```{r}
#| label: claims-plot
#| fig-cap: "Both routes. A bar is the difference in percent positive between the two NKG2C branches."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("claims_plot.png"))
```

## Part 5: clustering, a third route

Gating asks how many cells fall inside a boundary. Clustering asks how many groups
are in the data and what each one expresses. The second question needs no
hierarchy, so a population nobody thought to gate can still appear.

Debris, dead cells and doublets are removed by gating first, and the clustering
runs on the lymphocyte gate only. A cluster of debris is not a finding, and it
stretches the embedding so everything else is squeezed into a corner.

```{r}
#| label: umap-cell-types
#| fig-cap: "UMAP of the lymphocyte gate, coloured by the annotated cell type."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("umap_cell_types.png"))
```

### How a cluster gets a name

No cluster is named by eye. Each metacluster is scored against a definitions file
that gives the expected sign of each marker, and the best scoring definition wins.
The margin to the runner up is reported, so a close call is visible.

```{r}
#| label: cluster-annotation

annotation <- ReadOutput("cluster_annotation.csv")
kable(
  annotation[, c("cluster", "events", "percent_of_total", "cell_type",
                 "runner_up", "margin")],
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Each metacluster, its label, and how close the second choice was.",
  col.names = c("Metacluster", "Events", "Percent of gate", "Label",
                "Runner up", "Margin")
)
```

The score is a weighted mean over the markers a definition names, not a sum. That
distinction is not cosmetic. Under a sum, a definition is rewarded simply for
naming more markers: the adaptive NK definition names eight and the T cell
definition names two, so the adaptive label won every cluster, including the one
holding 88 percent of the file. The mean removes that.

```{r}
#| label: cluster-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Median marker expression per metacluster, scaled within each marker. This table drives the annotation."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("cluster_heatmap.png"))
```

```{r}
#| label: umap-markers
#| fig-cap: "The same embedding, coloured by each lineage marker. Read the labels against these panels."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("umap_markers.png"))
```

### Three routes, one file

```{r}
#| label: three-way

three_way <- ReadOutput("three_way_comparison.csv")
kable(
  three_way[, c("cell_type", "manual_percent", "automated_percent",
                "clustering_percent")],
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Every number is a percentage of the lymphocyte gate, so the three columns are comparable.",
  col.names = c("Cell type", "Manual gating", "Automated gating", "Clustering")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: three-way-plot
#| fig-cap: "The same table as a figure."

knitr::include_graphics(OutputImage("three_way_comparison.png"))
```

Clustering tracks automated gating closely on the largest population and
undercounts the small NK subsets. That is the expected failure mode: a rare
population is absorbed into a neighbouring metacluster, because the number of
metaclusters is chosen in advance and 12 is a guess.

The three columns disagree most where the population is smallest, which is also
where the biology of this paper sits. That is worth stating plainly rather than
presenting the agreement on T cells as if it settled the matter.

### What this shows and what it does not

It shows that an automated template reaches the same answer as a published expert
analysis on most populations of a real panel, and it names the one gate that
drives the difference.

It does not show that either method is right. There is no ground truth here, only
two analyses of the same file.

It also cannot say anything about analyst to analyst variation, which is the number
the literature reports. That needs the same files gated by many people. Maecker and
colleagues did exactly that with 15 laboratories and measured a mean CV of 20.5
percent under local gating against 4 percent under central gating [2]. One donor
file and two analyses cannot reproduce that design.

What one file can show is the direction. Whatever the template does, it does the
same thing every time it runs, and the reason it made each cut is in a CSV that a
reviewer can read.

## Reproducing this

```bash
# Pull this dataset only, not the 103 GB archive
./sync.sh pull datasets/flowrepository/OMIP-39

# Build the container. Every package version is pinned and asserted at build time.
./containers/build.sh

# The four analysis steps, in order
for step in 02_omip39_compensation_and_gating \
            03_compensation_method_sweep \
            04_omip39_reproduce_paper \
            05_omip39_clustering_umap; do
  podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
    Rscript "scripts/${step}.R"
done

# This report
podman run --rm -v "$PWD:/work:z" -w /work everything-flow-cytometry:latest \
  quarto render reports/omip39_automated_gating.qmd
```

```{r}
#| label: session-info

sessionInfo()
```
